summary: For Canadian SR&ED claimants, materials consumed are rendered virtually valueless, destroyed or scrapped by experimental work, while materials transformed are incorporated into another product, sub-assembly or prototype. Both are claimable under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) of the Income Tax Act, but transformed prototypes later sold or converted to commercial use trigger ITC recapture.

Executive Legal and Fiscal Architecture of Canadian R&D Incentives

Canada's primary fiscal mechanism for stimulating private-sector industrial research and technological innovation is the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, which represents the single largest federal government programme supporting business research and development in the country. During the 2025–2026 fiscal cycle, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) allowed $4.6 billion in SR&ED investment tax credits across 23,677 processed claims, underscoring the programme's central role in national industrial policy. Administered jointly by the Department of Finance Canada—which formulates legislative tax policy—and the CRA—which executes technical and financial compliance reviews—the programme operates through a dual-benefit statutory framework embedded within the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) (ITA) and the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945) (ITR).

Under the first statutory pillar, Section 37 of the ITA permits taxpayers carrying on business in Canada to pool eligible current expenditures and—following legislative restoration effective December 16, 2024—qualifying capital SR&ED expenditures, deducting them immediately in full against current-year business income or carrying the undeducted pool balance forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. Under the second statutory pillar, Section 127 and Section 127.1 of the ITA enable claimants to earn an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) ranging from a basic rate of 15% to an enhanced rate of 35% on qualified SR&ED expenditures. Depending on the legal status of the claimant, its prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada or three-year average annual gross revenue, and the nature of the underlying expenditure, earned ITCs may be applied to reduce Part I federal tax otherwise payable, refunded directly in cash, carried back three taxation years, or carried forward up to twenty taxation years.

Between December 2024 and March 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most consequential legislative transformation in over a decade. Initiated through the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, refined in the Department of Finance's August 15, 2025 draft legislative proposals, and enacted into law via Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, the federal government substantially expanded the generosity, reach, and capital intensity of the SR&ED regime retroactive to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Simultaneously, provincial jurisdictions—most notably Quebec through its 2025–2026 Budget introducing the Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025—restructured sub-national innovation incentives to capture capital equipment, pre-commercialization activities, and high-value technical labour.

body.text: Statutory Definition of SR&ED and Judicial Precedents
The Statutory Scope of Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

Eligibility for Canadian R&D tax incentives hinges on whether the underlying technical activities satisfy the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set out in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Designed to align broadly with the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) Frascati Manual, subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" encompassing three core pillars of scientific and technological inquiry. The first category, basic research under paragraph 248(1)(a), comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. The second category, applied research under paragraph 248(1)(b), encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. The third and commercially predominant category, experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c), covers work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, explicitly including incremental improvements thereto.

In addition to these three foundational categories, paragraph 248(1)(d) of the ITA extends statutory eligibility to specific categories of support work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer—restricted exclusively to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—where such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. This statutory enumeration is exhaustive rather than illustrative; any support activity not explicitly listed in paragraph 248(1)(d), or any enumerated activity whose scope exceeds what is strictly commensurate with the needs of the experimental investigation, is statutorily excluded from the SR&ED expenditure base.

Furthermore, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) of the ITA explicitly exclude activities that, while commercially vital or technically complex, do not involve resolving scientific or technological uncertainty through systematic experimentation. Statutorily excluded activities include market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection. These statutory exclusions establish a rigid legal boundary between the experimental resolution of technological uncertainty and the downstream commercial exploitation of resulting innovations.
Foundational Case Law and the Five Questions Framework

The statutory phrasing of subsection 248(1) of the ITA has been authoritatively interpreted by the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal. The bedrock judicial precedent governing SR&ED eligibility in Canada is Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839 (T.C.C.), written by Justice (later Chief Justice) Donald Bowman, and subsequently adopted as binding appellate law by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393. In Northwest Hydraulic, Chief Justice Bowman articulated a five-part analytical framework—universally referred to in Canadian tax practice and jurisprudence as the Five Questions—that a taxpayer must answer in the affirmative on a balance of probabilities to establish that claimed activities constitute SR&ED.

The first judicial criterion asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Chief Justice Bowman established that "routine engineering" encompasses techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the relevant scientific or technological field. Consequently, technological uncertainty is something that exists in the mind of the specialist; if the resolution of a technical problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures or publicly available engineering knowledge, no technological uncertainty exists. Crucially, commercial uncertainty, cost constraints, or uncertainty regarding whether a business objective can be met within budget do not constitute technological uncertainty under the Act.

The second and third judicial criteria examine the cognitive and methodological rigour of the investigation, asking whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty, and whether the procedure adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of the hypotheses. Satisfying these two criteria requires a structured, five-stage experimental progression: the observation of the underlying subject matter, the identification of the specific technological or scientific limitation, the formulation of a testable causal hypothesis explaining how and why a proposed intervention might overcome the limitation, the testing of that hypothesis through controlled experiment or analysis, and the logical evaluation or modification of the hypothesis based on experimental results. The investigation must be systematic rather than intuitive or haphazard shop-floor trial-and-error.

The fourth judicial criterion asks whether the process resulted in a technological advancement, defined as an advancement in the general understanding of science or technology. The advancement need not be a monumental breakthrough, as subsection 248(1) explicitly includes incremental improvements. However, the advancement must generate new scientific or technological knowledge that advances the baseline understanding of a competent professional in the field, rather than merely building a complex commercial product using known methods. Importantly, commercial or technical failure does not disqualify a project: if a systematic investigation fails to achieve its target performance parameters, it nevertheless achieves a technological advancement by proving that a hypothesized technical pathway is unviable under specific boundary conditions.

The fifth judicial criterion asks whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed. While the Tax Court of Canada has periodically accepted credible oral testimony to supplement gaps in written records, contemporaneous documentation generated during the execution of the research is treated by both the CRA and the courts as the primary evidentiary byproduct of the scientific method and the decisive proof that systematic experimentation occurred.
Evolution of Judicial Precedents and Administrative Policy Alignment

Beyond Northwest Hydraulic, a specialized body of Canadian tax jurisprudence governs specific evidentiary and procedural disputes in SR&ED audits, clarifying the boundaries of systematic investigation, software eligibility, and statutory filing deadlines.

body.text: In August 2021 (with subsequent updates through 2022–2026), the CRA consolidated its previous sector-specific eligibility policies into the unified Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives. In this administrative guidance, the CRA reorganized the five judicial questions into two overarching structural requirements—the "Why" requirement (that the work is conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement) and the "How" requirement (that the work is a systematic investigation or search carried out by means of experiment or analysis to overcome scientific or technological uncertainty). While CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) structure their audit inquiries around these two requirements (or the three operational pillars of technological uncertainty, systematic investigation, and technological advancement), the CRA explicitly acknowledges that both the two requirements and the five questions derive directly from subsection 248(1) of the ITA and Northwest Hydraulic. In any litigation before the Tax Court of Canada, as demonstrated in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King, the five Northwest Hydraulic questions remain the binding legal test.
Federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, and the 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms
Evolution from the 2024 Fall Economic Statement to Enacted Bill C-15 (Budget 2025)

A rigorous legal audit of Canadian SR&ED rates and thresholds requires distinguishing between three distinct chronological regimes and resolving an important legislative evolution between late 2024 and March 2026. In the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (and the accompanying August 15, 2025 Department of Finance draft legislative proposals), the federal government initially proposed raising the annual SR&ED expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3.0 million to $4.5 million. However, Budget 2025, which received Royal Assent and was enacted into law through Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) in March 2026, superseded that interim figure by doubling the annual expenditure limit from $3.0 million to $6.0 million, effective retroactively for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Consequently, while certain mid-2025 explanatory notes and transitional commentaries reference the interim $4.5 million proposal, the legally binding statutory expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.2) of the ITA and the CRA's updated Investment Tax Credit Policy for all taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, is $6.0 million, yielding a maximum enhanced refundable federal ITC of $2.1 million per year ($6,000,000 × 35%).

body.text: Mathematical Mechanics of the Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Formulas

Under subsection 127(10.2) of the ITA, for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the annual SR&ED expenditure limit for a Canadian-controlled private corporation (or an associated group of CCPCs under subsection 127(10.21)) using the default taxable capital method is determined by the statutory formula:

In this statutory equation, the variable A equals $0 (nil) whenever the corporation's (and all associated corporations') taxable capital employed in Canada for the immediately preceding taxation year is less than or equal to $15,000,000. Where prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000, variable A equals the lesser of $60,000,000 and the exact dollar amount by which the corporation's (and all associated corporations') prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000.

Expressed as a linear reduction rate, every $10 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada above the $15,000,000 threshold reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $1 (a 10% reduction slope), causing the expenditure limit to reach nil precisely when prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000. By contrast, for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the formula operated on a $3,000,000 base that phased out between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital (7.5% reduction slope).

Where a CCPC has a short taxation year (fewer than 365 days), subsection 127(10.5) of the ITA (renumbered from former subsection 127(10.6) by Bill C-15) mandates that the corporation's allocated expenditure limit be prorated by multiplying the otherwise determined limit by the ratio of the number of days in the short taxation year to 365. For example, if an associated CCPC is allocated $3,000,000 of the group's expenditure limit for a short taxation year running 184 days from July 1 to December 31, its effective expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.5) is reduced to $3,000,000 × (184 ÷ 365) = $1,512,328. Associated CCPCs must file an annual agreement on Schedule T2SCH49 under subsection 127(10.3) to allocate the group expenditure limit among members; if an associated group fails to file Schedule 49, the Minister of National Revenue is empowered under subsection 127(10.4) to allocate the limit among the corporations. Under paragraph 87(2)(j.6) of the ITA, continuity rules further stipulate that a new corporation formed as a result of an amalgamation is deemed to be a continuation of each predecessor corporation for the purpose of computing prior-year taxable capital and the subsection 127(10.2) expenditure limit.
Expansion to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and the CCPC Revenue Election

Prior to December 16, 2024, listing a Canadian technology or life-sciences company on a public stock exchange (such as the TSX, TSX Venture Exchange, NASDAQ, or NYSE) immediately terminated its CCPC status under subsection 125(7) of the ITA, stripping the company of the 35% refundable SR&ED credit and relegating it to the 15% non-refundable credit. To eliminate this structural disincentive against domestic public listings, Bill C-15 enacted the definition of an "eligible Canadian public corporation" (ECPC) in subsection 127(9) of the ITA and amended subsection 127(10.1) to grant ECPCs the enhanced 35% refundable ITC on up to $6.0 million of qualified expenditures for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024.

To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, a corporation must satisfy four cumulative statutory requirements. First, the corporation must be resident in Canada throughout the taxation year. Second, the corporation must have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange in Canada or abroad, or have elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation under subsection 89(1) of the ITA. Third, the corporation must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever—encompassing both de jure voting control and de facto control in fact under subsection 256(5.1) of the ITA—by one or more non-resident persons. Fourth, the corporation must not be controlled by a particular person if each share of its capital stock owned by a non-resident person were owned by that particular person, with non-resident holdings determined on the basis of publicly available information, including securities filings made before the year. Additionally, a Canadian-resident subsidiary corporation qualifies for ECPC treatment as an "eligible subsidiary" if not less than 90% of the issued shares of each class of its capital stock are owned, directly or indirectly, by one or more ECPCs throughout the taxation year.

Because public corporations do not compute associated CCPC taxable capital in the same manner as private corporations, subsections 127(10.6) and 127(10.62) of the ITA establish a revenue-based phase-out formula for ECPCs and consolidated ECPC groups. An ECPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced linearly based on its average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years, as reported in the audited financial statements of the corporation or—if the ECPC is a member of a corporate group that prepares consolidated financial statements as defined in subsection 233.8(1) of the ITA—the consolidated financial statements of the group:

where R is nil if the three-year average annual gross revenue is ≤ $15,000,000, and otherwise equals the excess of the three-year average annual gross revenue over $15,000,000 (capped at $60,000,000, reducing the expenditure limit to nil at $75,000,000 of average annual gross revenue). If an entity joins or leaves a consolidated ECPC group during the year, the average annual revenue used is that of the consolidated group as reflected in its consolidated financial statements for the year in question.

Crucially, under newly enacted subsection 127(10.31) (for a single CCPC) and subsection 127(10.32) (for an associated group of CCPCs), a CCPC may elect for any taxation year beginning on or after December 16, 2024, to compute its expenditure limit using the ECPC three-year average gross revenue method rather than the taxable capital method. Where an associated group of CCPCs makes this election under subsection 127(10.32), the taxable capital phase-out under subsection 127(10.2) ceases to apply for that year, and the group must aggregate the three-year average annual revenues reflected in the financial statements of every corporation that is a member of the associated group in the taxation year, regardless of whether those corporations were associated throughout the entire preceding three-year period.

This statutory election resolves a major structural distortion in Canadian venture finance. Under the default taxable capital method, capital-intensive biotechnology, clean-technology, semiconductor, and deep-tech startups that raise large equity or debt financing rounds (for example, $30 million to $65 million in preferred share capital) accumulate substantial "taxable capital employed in Canada" on their balance sheets long before generating commercial revenue. Under the legacy rules, such startups lost part or all of their 35% refundable SR&ED credit simply by holding cash or R&D assets funded by equity investors. By electing under subsection 127(10.31) or 127(10.32) to use the three-year average gross revenue test, a pre-revenue or early-revenue CCPC with $60 million in paid-up capital and $2 million in revenue retains 100% of its $6.0 million expenditure limit and $2.1 million annual cash refund.
Refundability Mechanics Under Section 127.1 and Taxability Under Paragraph 12(1)(t)

Earning an SR&ED ITC under Section 127 is legally distinct from having that ITC refunded in cash under Section 127.1 of the ITA. Any SR&ED ITC that is refunded to a claimant in a taxation year is deemed by subsection 127(5) to have been applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable, thereby reducing the pool of unused ITCs available for carryback or carryforward.

Under subsections 127.1(2) and 127.1(2.01) of the ITA, both qualifying CCPCs (as well as non-qualifying CCPCs that are not "excluded corporations" under subsection 127.1(2.01)) and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn a 100% cash refund on their 35% enhanced ITC attributable to current expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit, and a 40% cash refund on their 35% enhanced ITC attributable to restored capital expenditures acquired on or after December 16, 2024.

For SR&ED expenditures that exceed a corporation's annual expenditure limit (and therefore earn the 15% basic ITC), refundability diverges sharply between qualifying CCPCs, non-qualifying CCPCs, and ECPCs. A CCPC satisfies the statutory definition of a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2) of the ITA if its taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year (combined with the taxable incomes of all associated corporations) did not exceed its qualifying income limit. The baseline qualifying income limit is $500,000, which phases out linearly as the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the associated group increases from $15,000,000 to $75,000,000. If a CCPC satisfies this "qualifying corporation" test—for example, a startup with nil or ≤ $500,000 prior-year taxable income and < $75M prior-year taxable capital whose current-year R&D spending exceeds its expenditure limit—its 15% basic ITC earned on current and capital expenditures above the expenditure limit is 40% refundable, yielding an effective 6.0% cash refund (15% × 40%) on excess expenditures. Conversely, if a CCPC is not a "qualifying corporation" because its prior-year taxable income exceeded its qualifying income limit, subsection 127.1(2.01) still preserves 100% refundability on its 35% enhanced ITC for current expenditures (and 40% on capital expenditures) within its expenditure limit, provided it is not an "excluded corporation," but its 15% basic ITC on expenditures above the expenditure limit is 0% refundable. Similarly, for an ECPC, while the 35% enhanced ITC within the $6.0 million expenditure limit is 100% refundable on current expenditures and 40% refundable on capital expenditures, any 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures exceeding the ECPC's expenditure limit is 0% refundable.

For foreign-controlled corporations and non-eligible public corporations, all qualified SR&ED expenditures earn strictly the 15% basic ITC, which is 0% refundable. Unused non-refundable credits may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years under subsection 127(5) to offset Part I federal income tax payable. Individuals (sole proprietorships) and trusts each beneficiary of which is a qualifying corporation or an individual (other than a trust) also earn the 15% basic ITC, which is 40% refundable on unused credits remaining after offsetting Part I tax payable. Partnerships, because they are not distinct corporate taxpayers under the ITA, cannot earn the 35% enhanced ITC or claim a direct cash refund. Instead, under subsection 127(8) of the ITA, a partnership computes its qualified SR&ED expenditures at the end of its fiscal period—reducing its Section 37 expenditure pool by the ITC in the same year—and allocates the resulting 15% basic ITC to its active general partners in proportion to their partnership interests. Limited partners and tax-exempt partners are statutorily barred from receiving SR&ED ITC allocations under subsection 127(8) of the ITA (paragraph 127(8)(b) for specified members, including limited partners).

Finally, under paragraph 12(1)(t) of the ITA, any federal SR&ED ITC deducted against Part I tax payable or received as a cash refund in a taxation year (to the extent it does not directly reduce the Section 37 expenditure pool) must be included in the taxpayer's taxable income in the immediately following taxation year. This one-year deferral provides a cash-flow timing benefit to profitable claimants while ensuring that the net deductible business expense over the two-year cycle reflects only the unsubsidized portion of the R&D outlay.
Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies

To qualify for the Section 37 income deduction and the Section 127 ITC, an expenditure must first be incurred in respect of eligible SR&ED work under subsection 248(1) and must fall within the specific cost categories permitted under Section 37 and Section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR).
Salaries and Wages and Specified Employee Restrictions

Salaries and wages paid to employees who are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada constitute the foundation of most Canadian R&D claims. Whether an employee is "directly engaged" in SR&ED is determined strictly by the hands-on technical tasks performed—such as conducting experiments, building trial prototypes, writing experimental code, or providing direct first-line technical supervision of experimental work—and not by the employee's corporate job title. General administrative, clerical, human resources, finance, marketing, or C-suite executive management duties are ineligible.

Where an employee performs both SR&ED and non-SR&ED activities, salaries and wages (including the employer's share of statutory payroll levies such as Canada Pension Plan [CPP], Quebec Pension Plan [QPP], Employment Insurance [EI], and provincial workers' compensation or health payroll taxes) must be allocated based on contemporaneous time-tracking records. Furthermore, under subsection 37(1.5) of the ITA, salaries and wages paid to Canadian-resident employees performing SR&ED outside Canada are eligible, provided the foreign work is directly undertaken by the taxpayer (not subcontracted) and is solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada, up to a strict statutory cap equal to 10% of the total eligible salaries and wages directly attributable to SR&ED carried on in Canada.

Special statutory anti-avoidance caps apply to "specified employees"—defined in subsection 248(1) of the ITA as any employee who is a "specified shareholder" (owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, ≥ 10% of the issued shares of any class of the employer corporation or a related corporation) or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, child, or sibling of a controlling shareholder).

body.text: Overhead Calculation: Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) vs. Traditional Method

Taxpayers must make an irrevocable annual election in Part 3, Section A of Form T661 between two mutually exclusive methods for capturing SR&ED overhead expenditures: the Proxy Method (Line 160) or the Traditional Method (Line 162). Once filed for a taxation year, this election is legally binding and cannot be revoked or switched via an amended return for that year.

Elected by the vast majority of Canadian SR&ED claimants, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method under subsection 2900(4) of the ITR eliminates the administrative burden of tracking, apportioning, and substantiating individual overhead invoices. Under the Proxy Method, overhead and other expenditures at Line 360 of Form T661 are entered as zero, while actual overhead costs—such as facility rent, utilities, office supplies, and non-direct support salaries—remain fully deductible as ordinary business expenses under Section 9 of the ITA. In Part 5 of Form T661, the claimant calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) on Line 820 equal to 55% of the eligible salary base (Line 818). While the PPA rate was historically 65% for 2012 and prior years and 60% for 2013, it has been fixed at 55% since January 1, 2014, pursuant to subsection 2900(4) of the ITR. The resulting PPA is added directly to qualified expenditures in Part 4 of Form T661 for the purpose of earning the federal SR&ED ITC (as well as harmonized provincial credits such as Ontario's OITC and ORDTC and British Columbia's SR&ED credit), subject to an overall statutory cap ensuring the PPA does not exceed total business overhead expenses deducted in the year. Crucially, the 55% PPA is computed exclusively on the T4 salary base of directly engaged employees—excluding taxable benefits, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year under subsection 2900(9) of the ITR, and subject to the specified employee cap of the lesser of 75% of total wage or 2.5 × YMPE under subsection 2900(7) of the ITR. Payments to subcontractors and expenditures on materials never generate a proxy overhead uplift.

Conversely, under the Traditional Method (Line 162 of Form T661), no notional proxy amount is calculated. Instead, the claimant itemizes and claims actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661 that are directly attributable and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. In practice, electing the Traditional Method is mathematically advantageous only in capital- or facility-intensive operations where direct SR&ED labour is comparatively small relative to dedicated laboratory utilities, specialized shop consumables, or incremental R&D facility costs that exceed 55% of the direct salary base.
Materials Consumed or Transformed and Cloud Computing Expenses

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) of the ITA (read with subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) for proxy-method claimants and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the ITR for traditional-method claimants) and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, claimants may include the cost of materials that are either materials consumed—meaning they are rendered virtually valueless, destroyed, or scrapped as a direct result of the experimental process—or materials transformed, meaning they are incorporated into another product, sub-assembly, or experimental prototype during the prosecution of SR&ED.

In modern software, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and data-analytics SR&ED claims, cloud computing infrastructure costs—such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud Platform (GCP), and Microsoft Azure—used directly and exclusively for R&D experimentation, model training, staging, and experimental testing environments qualify as eligible SR&ED expenses (claimed as materials consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED or directly attributable R&D expenses in accordance with CRA guidelines). However, the CRA enforces a strict audit boundary on cloud and API expenditures: claimants must maintain separate cloud accounts or rigorous cost-centre segmentation in the general ledger to isolate experimental R&D development/staging environments (eligible) from commercial production and live customer hosting environments (Cost of Goods Sold [COGS], which are strictly ineligible). Coding commercial production hosting or live customer third-party API calls to R&D expense accounts distorts both gross margin and the SR&ED base, triggering immediate disallowances during a CRA financial review.

Furthermore, where physical materials are transformed into a custom experimental prototype, pilot plant, or trial batch that is subsequently sold to a customer or converted to commercial use, the initial material expenditure may be claimed in the year incurred, but ITC recapture rules under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the ITA are triggered in the subsequent taxation year in which the prototype or transformed material is sold or converted to commercial use. The recapture mechanism claws back previously claimed tax benefits by adding directly to Part I federal tax payable the lesser of the ITC originally earned on the property and the applicable ITC percentage multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value upon conversion to commercial use).
Subcontractor and Third-Party Payments (The 80% Inclusion Rule)

When a claimant contracts out eligible SR&ED work to an arm's-length Canadian subcontractor performing basic research, applied research, experimental development, or eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work in Canada on the claimant's behalf, or makes a third-party payment under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.01) to (iii) of the ITA to an approved association, university, college, research institute, or non-profit R&D organization in Canada where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results, two distinct statutory inclusion rates apply. For income tax deduction purposes under Section 37 of the ITA, 100% of the eligible arm's-length SR&ED contract or third-party payment is deductible in the year or added to the Section 37 pool. For investment tax credit purposes, however, pursuant to subparagraph (a)(ii) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA (applicable after 2012), only 80% of the eligible arm's-length contract payment or third-party payment is included in qualified expenditures when computing the federal SR&ED ITC. This statutory 20% reduction strips the subcontractor's assumed profit margin and overhead markup from the tax credit base.

To substantiate an arm's-length SR&ED contract during a CRA review, the claimant must maintain a written contract executed prior to or during the work that explicitly specifies the technical SR&ED tasks to be performed in Canada, confirms that the work was physically performed within Canada (as payments to foreign contractors for work performed outside Canada are 0% eligible), demonstrates that only hands-on technical SR&ED work is claimed (excluding project management, commercial UI/UX design, or routine deployment), and confirms that the claimant retains ownership or the right to exploit the resulting intellectual property. For non-arm's length (NAL) subcontractors, the 80% inclusion rule does not apply; instead, under subsections 127(11.6) and 127(13) to (15) of the ITA, contract payments between non-arm's length parties are excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures, and the performing NAL entity claims its own underlying direct SR&ED costs (or transfers qualified expenditures via a formal statutory agreement).
Restoration of Capital Expenditures (Effective December 16, 2024)

After being repealed for an eleven-year period running from January 1, 2014, through December 15, 2024, capital expenditures for SR&ED have been restored under paragraph 37(1)(b), subsection 127(9), and subsection 127.1(2) of the ITA, effective for new depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, and lease costs that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024. Capital expenditures made or deemed to have been made before December 16, 2024, remain strictly ineligible for both the Section 37 deduction and the Section 127 ITC.

To qualify as an eligible SR&ED capital expenditure under the restored regime, the acquired machinery, equipment, or apparatus—such as laboratory instruments, prototyping machinery, testing rigs, and eligible classes of data network infrastructure or electronic data-processing equipment—must be new to the claimant and used in Canada. Crucially, at the time of acquisition, the property must satisfy the strict "all or substantially all" (≥ 90%) threshold, meaning the taxpayer must demonstrate an intention either to use the property all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the performance of SR&ED in Canada, or to consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value in the performance of SR&ED in Canada. While the pre-2014 regime briefly permitted partial claims for "first term" and "second term" shared-use equipment under subsections 127(18) to (20), the restored post-December 15, 2024 rules require satisfying the ≥ 90% SR&ED threshold. Furthermore, the acquisition or leasing of land, buildings, or leasehold interests in buildings remains categorically excluded from SR&ED eligibility.

Qualifying capital expenditures are 100% immediately deductible against business income under paragraph 37(1)(b) of the ITA and earn the 35% enhanced ITC (for CCPCs and ECPCs within their $6.0 million expenditure limit) or the 15% basic ITC. However, under subsection 127.1(2) of the ITA, the refundability rate on the 35% ITC earned on capital expenditures is capped at 40%, yielding an immediate 14.0% cash refund on capital equipment (35% × 40%), with the remaining 21.0% non-refundable credit available to offset Part I tax payable or carry forward 20 years. If the SR&ED capital asset is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, both capital cost allowance (CCA) / Section 37 recapture and Section 127 ITC recapture rules apply to recover the previously claimed tax benefits.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Incentives and Stacking Mechanics
The Government Assistance Grind (Subsection 127(18) of the Income Tax Act)

In Canada, corporations may legally stack provincial or territorial R&D tax credits—as well as federal or provincial innovation grants such as the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), CanExport SMEs, or Investissement Québec ESSOR contributions—on top of the federal SR&ED ITC. However, under subsections 127(18) to 127(20) of the ITA and the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits, forgivable loans, and government grants received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received in respect of SR&ED constitute "government assistance".

Under subsection 127(18) of the ITA, government assistance reduces the taxpayer's pool of federal qualified SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar before the federal 35% or 15% ITC rate is applied. Where the amount of assistance and contract payments relating to a project exceeds the total qualified SR&ED expenditures of that project, subsection 127(19) reduces the qualified expenditures of the claimant and any non-arm's length party to nil. Two vital technical principles govern the interaction between provincial credits and the federal calculation. First, while a provincial R&D tax credit reduces the overall pool of federal qualified expenditures on Form T661 (Part 4) and Schedule 31, receiving a provincial R&D tax credit does not reduce the salary base used to compute the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount in Part 5 of Form T661. By contrast, a direct wage subsidy or grant (such as an NRC IRAP salary contribution) reduces the net deductible SR&ED expenditure pool directly. Second, in Ontario, because the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) reduces the eligible expenditure base for both the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) and the federal SR&ED ITC, the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy (Appendices A.1, A.2, and A.3) sets out exact calculation sequences to account for both credits simultaneously.

body.text: Quebec's 2025–2026 CRIC Overhaul and the DICI Patent Box

In the Quebec 2025–2026 Budget tabled on March 25, 2025 (and further detailed in Revenu Québec's fiscal bulletin published on July 9, 2025), the Government of Quebec executed a fundamental restructuring of its provincial innovation tax regime, committing $271.5 million in net additional financial support over five years. For taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec abolished its fragmented suite of legacy R&D tax measures—specifically terminating the traditional R&D salary tax credit, the university/public research centre R&D credit, the private partnership pre-competitive research credit, the research consortium fees credit, the technological adaptation services credit, the industrial design tax credit, and the tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts.

In their place, Quebec established the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC — Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation / précommercialisation), administered independently by Revenu Québec. Unlike the abolished Quebec R&D salary tax credit—where the enhanced 30% rate phased down based on consolidated world assets—the CRIC provides a 30% fully refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold for every eligible corporation, regardless of whether the company is a CCPC, a large domestic public company, or a foreign-controlled multinational subsidiary operating an establishment in Quebec. Eligible expenditures exceeding that first $1,000,000 tier earn a 20% fully refundable credit with no ceiling. According to Quebec Ministry of Finance modelling, for a large corporation executing a $5 million innovation project in Quebec, the CRIC delivers 90% more fiscal assistance than the abolished regime.

In addition to traditional R&D salaries, the CRIC expands the provincial tax base across two new dimensions. First, expenditures dedicated to pre-commercialization activities—such as regulatory compliance testing, certification trials, industrial design for manufacturability, and product validation—qualify for the CRIC, subject to the condition that pre-commercialization activities must be undertaken in conjunction with R&D work carried out in Quebec by the corporation or on its behalf. Second, the CRIC covers 100% of eligible capital equipment (CAPEX) acquired for R&D or eligible pre-commercialization activities in Quebec (excluding land and buildings). At the same time, whereas the legacy Quebec regime applied varying inclusion rates to different classes of subcontractors, the CRIC standardizes all eligible subcontracting contracts at a single 50% inclusion rate, regardless of whether the subcontractor is an arm's-length private R&D service provider, a university, a College Centre for the Transfer of Technologies (CCTT), or a research consortium. This 50% inclusion rate ensures tax neutrality with in-house R&D, as subcontractor invoices bundle overhead and material costs that are not directly eligible under the CRIC.

To focus fiscal support on higher-value-added technical jobs, the CRIC applies a modified annual exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the employee thresholds for R&D and pre-commercialization personnel ($18,571 per eligible employee, prorated by the percentage of time each employee devotes to qualifying R&D and pre-commercialization activities during the year). Where an eligible corporation or partnership claims more than one Quebec tax credit subject to an exclusion threshold, specific coordination rules govern the threshold allocation, while the Quebec nexus ratio for the Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations in Quebec (DICI) is explicitly protected from reduction by the CRIC exclusion threshold. Under the DICI—which serves as the second pillar of Quebec's reformed innovation regime alongside the CRIC and represents 7.3% of Quebec's innovation tax support—corporations operating an establishment in Quebec that derive income from commercializing qualified intellectual property assets developed in Quebec benefit from an effective Quebec corporate income tax rate of 2% on eligible commercialization profits.
Worked Financial Stacking Analyses: Ontario and Quebec CCPC Case Studies

To illustrate the exact statutory arithmetic of federal-provincial credit stacking, proxy overhead calculation, subcontractor 80% (federal) vs. 50% (Quebec CRIC) inclusion rules, and the subsection 127(18) government assistance grind, consider a qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) in its 2026 taxation year (beginning after March 25, 2025) with prior-year taxable capital below $15 million and prior-year taxable income below $500,000. Filing Procedures, Pre-Claim Advisory Services, and CRA Audit Mechanics
Statutory Filing Forms and the Hard 18-Month Deadline

To claim federal SR&ED tax incentives, a taxpayer must submit a complete prescribed filing package to the CRA along with its income tax return. The primary technical and financial return is Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), prepared in accordance with Guide T4088. Form T661 captures general corporate information (Part 1), detailed project-by-project technical narratives addressing scientific or technological uncertainties, systematic investigations, and advancements (Part 2), calculation of allowable Section 37 SR&ED expenditures and the Section 37 pool balance (Part 3), calculation of qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes (Part 4), calculation of the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Part 5), project-level cost breakdowns (Part 6), statistical data for Statistics Canada (Part 7), claim checklist (Part 8), mandatory claim preparer information and fee arrangements (Part 9), and corporate certification (Part 10). Because Form T661 calculates only the deductible expenditure pool and the qualified expenditure base rather than the monetary tax credit itself, corporations must simultaneously file Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations)—along with Schedule T2SCH49 if allocating the expenditure limit among associated CCPCs—while unincorporated individuals file Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)).

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the ITA, a claimant's prescribed forms (Form T661 and Schedule 31 or Form T2038(IND)) must be filed on or before the SR&ED reporting deadline, which is strictly defined as 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. For a corporation, because the T2 corporate income tax return is due 6 months after the end of its fiscal taxation year, adding 12 months establishes a strict statutory deadline of 18 months from the end of the fiscal year; for instance, a corporation with a December 31, 2024 fiscal year-end has a T2 filing due date of June 30, 2025, and an absolute SR&ED filing deadline of June 30, 2026. For an individual carrying on an unincorporated business, the T1 return is due June 15 of the following calendar year, yielding an SR&ED filing deadline of June 15 of the second following year (17.5 months after the December 31 year-end), whereas for a trust, the T3 return is due 90 days after the trust's year-end, yielding a 15-month SR&ED reporting deadline.

As confirmed repeatedly by the Tax Court of Canada—including in Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 211, aff'd 2016 FCA 301, where a Schedule 31 filed after the deadline barred the ITC even though Form T661 had been filed on time—the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline is a strict statutory bar ("hard deadline"). The ministerial taxpayer relief provisions of the ITA do not authorize the CRA to grant extensions to the 18-month window. If a claimant misses the 18-month deadline by even a single day—unless the deadline falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or CRA-recognized public holiday, in which case it shifts to the next business day—both the Section 37 deduction and the Section 127 ITC for that year are permanently forfeited. Consequently, tax practitioners strongly advise filing the SR&ED claim with the initial T2 return within 6 months of fiscal year-end, leaving a 12-month buffer during which the claimant can file an amended Form T661 or Schedule 31 if additional qualifying expenditures are identified prior to the 18-month cutoff. Furthermore, under subsection 162(5.1) of the ITA, Part 9 of Form T661 requires mandatory disclosure of whether any external claim preparer participated in preparing the claim, their Business Number, and whether they charged a contingency fee—which typically ranges between 15% and 25% of the refund in the Canadian market—or a flat fee, with a $1,000 penalty applicable for incomplete or inaccurate preparer disclosure.
CRA Service Standards and Pre-Claim Advisory Services

Once a complete SR&ED claim is submitted, the CRA measures its processing turnaround against published Service Standards. Claims (refundable or non-refundable) that are Accepted as Filed without an audit review are processed within a service standard of 60 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim (with typical administrative turnaround averaging five to eight weeks when not under heavy load). Refundable claims that are selected for a technical and/or financial review carry a service standard of 180 calendar days (roughly 24 weeks) from receipt, while the former 365-calendar-day standard for non-refundable claims and claimant-requested adjustments to non-refundable claims applies only to complete claims received before April 1, 2018.

To enhance predictability and help businesses establish compliant documentation practices before filing, the CRA offers four free upstream advisory tools and services, having replaced the legacy Pre-Claim Project Review (PCPR) programme with the modern Pre-Claim Consultation (PCC) and Pre-Claim Review (PCR) services.

body.text: CRA Coordinated Audit Mechanics: The Claim Review Manual (CRM) and Financial Claim Review Manual (FCRM)

When an SR&ED claim is filed with a CRA Tax Centre, automated risk-scoring algorithms and screening officers determine whether the claim can be Accepted as Filed (AAF) or must be referred to a Coordinating Tax Services Office (CTSO) for detailed examination. Within the CTSO, the Control Function evaluates the referral and assigns the file to a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA)—a domain-credentialed scientist or engineer trained under CRA courses TD 1170-000 and HQ1188-000 through HQ1183-000 and supervised by a Research and Technology Manager (RTM)—and a Financial Reviewer (FR).

The conduct of all CRA technical and financial audits is strictly governed by two public administrative manuals: the Claim Review Manual (CRM) for Research and Technology Advisors and the Financial Claim Review Manual (FCRM) – Review Procedures for Financial Reviewers. Under the CRM and the FCRM, the RTA and FR are mandated to execute a Coordinated Review, a collaborative process designed to resolve overlapping compliance issues while minimizing administrative disruption to the claimant. Early in the review process, the RTA and FR communicate their planned audit scope, share prior-year claim histories (including any FTCAS or PCC files), and identify joint technical-financial issues—such as verifying whether specific employees or subcontractors performed hands-on SR&ED tasks, assessing whether materials were consumed or transformed, or evaluating whether capital equipment met the ≥ 90% SR&ED usage threshold. The RTA must prepare a written Review Plan detailing the scope, major issues, and methodology required to resolve those concerns.

To avoid asking the claimant for the same documentation twice, the RTA and FR coordinate their Requests for Information (RFIs) and schedule a joint on-site or virtual review visit. During the review meeting—which the CRM emphasizes must be attended by the claimant's technical personnel most familiar with the work done—the RTA examines the claimant's Business Context (BC), technological baseline, experimental logs, source-code repositories (Git commits, sprint logs, architecture decision records), test bench data, and failure analyses, while the FR reconciles Part 3, Part 4, and Part 5 of Form T661 against T4 payroll summaries, timesheets, general ledger accounts, and subcontractor contracts. At the conclusion of the site visit, the RTA provides a preliminary verbal indication of their eligibility findings so the claimant has a fair opportunity to bring forward additional representations or contemporaneous records.

Section 1.6.0 of the CRM enforces strict due-process safeguards grounded in the Taxpayer Bill of Rights. Specifically, RTAs are strictly prohibited from negotiating eligibility or expenditure percentages with claimants; all determinations must rest on objective evidence and statutory requirements. Furthermore, an RTA is strictly required by Section 1.6.0 of the CRM to consult their Research and Technology Manager (RTM) before disallowing a claim for lack of information, before making any unfavourable eligibility decision without conducting an on-site visit, whenever significant modifications are made to the Review Plan, when contentious policy questions arise, or where penalties or suspected fraud are involved.

Following the technical review, the RTA drafts the formal SR&ED Review Report (maintained in the CRA's TF98 file and tracked statistically in the Audit Information Management System [AIMS]). Before issuing the report to the claimant, the RTA must provide the draft SR&ED Review Report to the FR for examination and feedback to ensure all joint technical-financial observations—such as whether an employee noted during technical interviews was a shareholder and therefore a "specified employee"—are accurately communicated without the RTA making strictly financial determinations. In Section 5.1 / 6.8.2 of the SR&ED Review Report, every claimed project is assigned a formal AIMS determination code:

body.text: If the RTA and FR propose negative adjustments, due-process rules require issuing a formal Proposal Package enclosing the RTA's SR&ED Review Report and the FR's financial proposal letter, granting the claimant 30 days to submit a written rebuttal or additional documentary evidence. If disagreements persist after the RTA and FR respond to the claimant's rebuttal, the claimant may escalate the dispute through the CRA's administrative dispute resolution hierarchy—first to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and Financial Review Manager (FRM), and subsequently to the SR&ED Assistant Director at the CTSO—prior to the issuance of a formal Notice of Assessment or Reassessment. Once a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, a claimant has 90 days from the date of mailing to file a formal Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch, which conducts an independent review (and, where prior-year objections overlap with a current-year audit, the claimant may request that the current review be held in abeyance in AIMS pending the Appeals decision). If the Appeals Branch confirms the disallowance, the claimant may appeal directly to the Tax Court of Canada, whose judgment—subject only to appellate review by the Federal Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court of Canada—is final.
Strategic Conclusions and Audit Readiness Recommendations

By doubling the federal enhanced 35% expenditure limit to $6.0 million under Bill C-15, widening the CCPC phase-out range to $15 million–$75 million, introducing the subsection 127(10.31)/(10.32) gross revenue election for CCPCs, extending the 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restoring capital expenditures after an eleven-year absence, Parliament has removed the historical fiscal penalties that hampered scaling Canadian technology and manufacturing enterprises. Concurrently, Quebec's transition to the universally refundable 30%/20% CRIC regime—incorporating pre-commercialization activities and 100% CAPEX alongside the 2% DICI patent box—establishes one of the most competitive sub-national innovation environments in the OECD.

To capture these expanded tax incentives while insulating claims against CRA adjustments during Coordinated Reviews, corporate claimants and tax auditors must integrate four rigorous governance protocols into their annual tax compliance cycle. First, scaling private corporations whose prior-year associated taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15 million should perform an annual comparative calculation between subsection 127(10.2) (the default taxable capital method) and subsection 127(10.31)/(10.32) (the three-year average annual gross revenue election) prior to filing Schedule 31 and Schedule 49, as venture-capitalized pre-revenue or early-revenue CCPCs electing the gross revenue method preserve up to $2.1 million in annual refundable federal credits that would otherwise be eroded by balance-sheet equity. Second, because restored capital expenditures (for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024) require proving all or substantially all (≥ 90%) usage in SR&ED over the asset's expected useful life, claimants must maintain dated acquisition invoices, commissioning logs, and equipment utilization schedules from the date of purchase, while software and AI enterprises claiming cloud computing costs as materials consumed must maintain strict general-ledger and cloud-account separation between experimental training/staging environments and commercial production (COGS) workloads.

Third, because owner-managers and ≥ 10% shareholders ("specified employees") cannot claim dividends, management fees, bonuses, or profit-based remuneration for SR&ED, and are capped at the lesser of 75% of total T4 wages or 2.5 × YMPE for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount salary base, technical founders must be placed on regular T4 base payroll paid within 180 days of fiscal year-end to avoid forfeiture under subsection 78(4) of the ITA and subsections 2900(7) and 2900(9) of the ITR. Finally, rather than reconstructing project narratives retrospectively at year-end, engineering teams should embed lightweight contemporaneous tracking into existing agile workflows—tagging sprint tickets, architecture decision records, failed hypothesis branches, and benchmark test logs to specific technological uncertainties as the work progresses. When a claim is selected for a CRA Coordinated Review, presenting chronological, contemporaneous experimental records that directly answer the five Northwest Hydraulic questions remains the decisive factor in securing an "All Work Eligible" (AW) determination.
